article_title: A Hybrid Collaborative Filtering and Knowledge Graph-Based Cross-Domain Recommendation Method for Multimodal Teaching Resources
citation: Bin Liu, Xiaoli Sun, Jia Song. (2026). A hybrid collaborative filtering and knowledge graph-based cross-domain recommendation method for multimodal teaching resources. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100678
title: Pedagogically structured knowledge graph with four instructional dimensions and ability/progress-aware CF fusion
description: The framework organizes teaching resources, concepts, and learner attributes in a knowledge graph whose relations fall into three categories (content/domain, skill/goal, and pedagogical-alignment relations). Each resource entity is decomposed into four instructional dimensions — teaching context, cognitive level, technological feature, and cultural adaptability — whose embeddings yield dimension-specific cosine similarities combined into user-dependent semantic similarity via attention weights. An adaptive fusion coefficient λu, computed from learner ability (LAE), progress (LPT), and interest (IPI) indices, balances semantic and behavioral scores so that "A learner with higher ability, more stable progress and stronger overall interest receives a larger λu". The recommendation process runs from explicit instructional requirements through KG semantic expansion, CF refinement, and score fusion.
requirements: Resource metadata normalized into a unified schema and mapped into the knowledge graph
Learner interaction logs with view duration, completion ratio, and click signals to construct IPI, LAE, and LPT indices
Explicit instructional requirements (domain, skills, difficulty, modality, cultural preferences) encoded as a query vector
constraints: The schema is kept fixed across all experiments and can be extended when additional pedagogical metadata become available
All evaluations are on historical interaction logs; reported improvements reflect recommendation quality rather than educational or learning effectiveness
target_learners: English language learners in classroom, blended, and self-directed study scenarios
target_learning_goals: Matching multimodal English teaching resources to learner ability, progress, and instructional requirements across domains
examples: Resources carry metadata such as the example 'Past Tense in Narratives' mapped to triples like 'aligned with cognitive level Apply' and 'suitable for context Self-study'
key_sources: Bin Liu, Xiaoli Sun, Jia Song. (2026). A hybrid collaborative filtering and knowledge graph-based cross-domain recommendation method for multimodal teaching resources. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100678

article_title: A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments
citation: Stephanie Frost · Gord McCalla. (2020). A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00221-3
title: CFLS planner: collaborative filtering on learning sequences for open-ended pedagogical planning
description: The CFLS planner is a pedagogical planning algorithm designed for open-ended, unstructured learning environments based on the ecological approach architecture. It builds a neighbourhood of learners who followed a similar sequence of the b most recent learning objects as a target learner, then recommends the most successful forward path of f learning objects drawn from those neighbours' subsequent histories. Success is judged through analysis of interaction data (average P[learned] on the forward path) rather than external metadata. The planner requires no externally engineered metadata about learning objects and no structured learner model in advance, since all relationships are derived from learner behaviour traces captured on learning objects.
requirements: Accumulated usage data from prior learners in the environment to enable neighbourhood formation
constraints: Suffers a cold start problem when insufficient usage data is available
Neighbourhood matching approach (exact sequence match, set match, or partial order) depends on the density of data available
target_learners: self-directed learners in open-ended, unstructured learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized guidance on learning goal setting and achievement through recommended learning object sequences
examples: In the simulation, the CFLS planner matched learners using a set match with pass/fail outcome correspondence and recommended the path with the highest average P[learned] among neighbours.
key_sources: Stephanie Frost · Gord McCalla. (2020). A Planning Algorithm to Support Learning in Open-ended, Unstructured Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00221-3

article_title: Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs
citation: Hu, Y., & Spiro, R.J. (2021). Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09920-z
title: Cognitive flexibility theory as an epistemic lens for online learning design
description: Cognitive flexibility theory (CFT) is presented as a lens for reflecting on MOOC and online learning design. The article states that "The need for such a reframing is a tenet of CFT", positioning CFT as an epistemic framework that calls for reorienting the standpoint of online learning. The authors use CFT to reflect on proposals to combine c-MOOC and xMOOC designs and to inform future design and practice of MOOCs and online learning generally, aiming at the development of adaptive worldviews.
requirements: Designers must adopt a CFT-based epistemic stance rather than treating online learning as a purely logistical delivery problem
constraints: The article applies CFT in the context of pandemic-induced emergency remote teaching and MOOCs
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs and emergency remote teaching
examples: The authors use CFT as a lens to reflect on the Loizzo and Ertmer proposal to combine c-MOOC and xMOOC designs
key_sources: Hu, Y., & Spiro, R.J. (2021). Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09920-z

article_title: Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs
citation: Hu, Y., & Spiro, R.J. (2021). Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09920-z
title: Apply CFT learning and instruction principles as a principled overlay when designing online learning under urgent conditions
description: The article recommends holding CFT in mind as a principled overlay while urgently preparing for current schooling, so that online learning is built better for now and for longer-term needs. It states: "Having this framework in mind as a principled overlay while urgently preparing for current schooling can help us build better, for now". Application of CFT learning and instruction principles is presented as benefiting online learning for the development of adaptive worldviews and adaptive skill.
requirements: Designers must know and apply the learning and instruction principles of CFT
constraints: Framed for pandemic-induced emergency remote teaching and online learning generally
examples: The authors present examples of ways application of CFT learning and instruction principles can benefit online learning
key_sources: Hu, Y., & Spiro, R.J. (2021). Design for now, but with the future in mind: a “cognitive flexibility theory” perspective on online learning through the lens of MOOCs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09920-z

article_title: Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations
citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: CFFD chart for multi-dimensional collaboration documentation
description: The CFFD chart provides a Chronologically ordered record of Features in use, Focus of interactivity and Dialogue, extending CORDFU to four dimensions of collaboration: software features and on-screen dialogue, dialogue between children or researcher and children, children's use of toy features and dialogue with the toy, and interactions between toy and software. Each horizontal line shows one of the categories of speech and action performed by the researcher, the children, the toy and the software, and the links between the horizontal lines indicate the interactions between the participants along these dimensions.
requirements: The locus of the Features Used must be differentiated to specify at which interface they occur, toy or software
constraints: As yet it is early days for the CACHET project data analysis and the documentation techniques being developed are very much work in progress
examples: Figure 6 illustrates a small section of a CFFD chart for two children using the toy and software
key_sources: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/

article_title: Barriers and facilitators to implementing e-learning for infection management in primary care: a scoping review.
citation: Jørgensen Louise Bidstrup, Jensen Jette Nygaard, Clausen Caroline Skovsbo, Kousgaard Marius Brostrøm, Arnold Sif Helene. (2026). Barriers and facilitators to implementing e-learning for infection management in primary care: a scoping review. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03385-4
title: CFIR five-domain mapping as the organizing framework for e-learning implementation determinants
description: The review uses the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to code and organize implementation determinants. Determinants were "mapped across CFIR’s five domains (Innovation, Outer setting, Inner setting, Individuals, and Implementation process)", coded one at a time to the domain, subdomain, and construct best reflecting the original description, with two researchers coding independently and discrepancies resolved by consensus. In this review it serves as the synthesis structure for facilitators and barriers.
requirements: Determinants must be explicitly described in original studies as influencing implementation, uptake, or use of the e-learning intervention positively or negatively
constraints: The review maps reported determinants rather than evaluating strength of evidence; no formal methodological quality appraisal was conducted
target_learners: healthcare professionals in primary care, including GPs, nurses, and pharmacists
target_learning_goals: implementation and sustained use of e-learning interventions for infection management
examples: Determinants such as self-paced access, mobile-ready design, firewall restrictions, and the Commitment-to-Change method were each mapped to specific CFIR constructs in Appendix 2
key_sources: Jørgensen Louise Bidstrup, Jensen Jette Nygaard, Clausen Caroline Skovsbo, Kousgaard Marius Brostrøm, Arnold Sif Helene. (2026). Barriers and facilitators to implementing e-learning for infection management in primary care: a scoping review. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03385-4

article_title: Research in Mathematics Educational Technology: Current Trends and Futrue Demands
citation: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. In Wiest, L. R., & Lamberg, T. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education (pp. 373-380). Reno, NV: University of Nevada, Reno.
title: Comprehensive Framework of Teacher Knowledge (CFTK)
description: The Comprehensive Framework of Teacher Knowledge (CFTK) is a three-dimensional model for addressing multiple aspects of teacher knowledge and their interactions. It transforms current understanding of teacher knowledge from a linear structure to a three-dimensional model by pairing six inter-related aspects into three orthogonal axes: Field (Subject Matter and Pedagogy), Mode (Orientation and Discernment), and Context (Individual and Environment). The review applies CFTK as one of three frameworks for analyzing mathematics educational technology research.
requirements: Detailed description of CFTK aspects and dimensions available in Ronau and Rakes (in press)
target_learning_goals: Understanding teacher knowledge for technology integration in mathematics
key_sources: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. In Wiest, L. R., & Lamberg, T. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education (pp. 373-380). article_title: Moderators' Role in Fostering Health Practitioner Engagement Within an Online Active Learning Program (The Community Fracture Capture Learning Hub): Qualitative Relational Content Thematic Analysis.
citation: Stone Alicia, Enaworu Oghenetanure, Wilson Iseult, Fathalla Ahmed M, Chang Shanton, Audehm Ralph, Chiang Cherie, Gorelik Alexandra, Yates Christopher J, Snow Steve, Barmanray Rahul D, Price Sarah, Collins Lucy, Wark John D. (2026). Moderators' Role in Fostering Health Practitioner Engagement Within an Online Active Learning Program (The Community Fracture Capture Learning Hub): Qualitative Relational Content Thematic Analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/83764
title: Community Fracture Capture (CFC) Learning Hub
description: The CFC Learning Hub is a secure, adaptable web-based platform for case-based, interactive small-group learning on osteoporosis management, delivered through the Praxhub platform to primary care physicians. Central to its design is "an interactive Discussion Forum that encourages participant engagement and peer-to-peer exchange on course material," guided by experienced PCP moderators supported by specialist moderators. Between May 2022 and October 2023 it ran four 6-week cycles involving 55 PCPs in groups of 12 to 16, with 33 (60%) actively commenting or asking questions.
requirements: PCP and specialist moderators active simultaneously to guide discussions and select case content
constraints: Designed to address the osteoporosis treatment gap in community settings; participation was voluntary and uncompensated
target_learners: Primary care physicians across a range of professional backgrounds and experience levels
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based bone health and osteoporosis management in primary care
examples: Over 630 comments, 160 pages, and more than 53,000 words of weekly discussions were compiled for qualitative analysis

(2026). Moderators' Role in Fostering Health Practitioner Engagement Within an Online Active Learning Program (The Community Fracture Capture Learning Hub): Qualitative Relational Content Thematic Analysis. article_title: Midwives' knowledge and perspectives on neonatal resuscitation and survival before and after Helping Babies Breathe training: a qualitative study in Uganda.
citation: Myrnerts Höök Susanna, Abrahamsson Marielle, Namusoko Sarah, Byamugisha Josaphat, Bergström Anna. (2025). Midwives' knowledge and perspectives on neonatal resuscitation and survival before and after Helping Babies Breathe training: a qualitative study in Uganda. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094012
title: Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) as a lens for identifying barriers to implementing HBB
description: The article uses the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research as an analytical lens for understanding why evidence-based practices such as HBB are difficult to implement in routine care. It states that CFIR "offer[s] a lens through which implementers can identify areas needing attention", covering characteristics of the implemented method, the roles and attributes of targeted individuals, the setting, and the implementation process. In this study, challenges were identified across all CFIR domains and were not isolated to HBB itself, spanning referral systems, working culture, recognition, and psychological and physical safety.
requirements: Implementation analysis must attend to the method, the individuals targeted, the setting and the implementation process, as the framework's domains specify
constraints: In this study the framework was applied retrospectively to qualitative data from a single referral hospital's high-risk labour ward and theatre
target_learners: midwives and other health workers implementing neonatal resuscitation training in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: adopting and sustaining evidence-based neonatal resuscitation practices such as HBB
examples: The study mapped midwives' reported challenges onto CFIR domains, finding barriers in context (referral delays, working culture), individuals, and the implementation process
key_sources: Myrnerts Höök Susanna, Abrahamsson Marielle, Namusoko Sarah, Byamugisha Josaphat, Bergström Anna. (2025). Midwives' knowledge and perspectives on neonatal resuscitation and survival before and after Helping Babies Breathe training: a qualitative study in Uganda. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094012

article_title: Assessing competence of primary care respiratory healthcare professionals to deliver a psychologically-based intervention for people with COPD: results from the TANDEM study.
citation: Wileman V., Steed L., Pinnock H., Kelly M., Sohanpal R., Heslop-Marshall K., Taylor SJC. (2025). Assessing competence of primary care respiratory healthcare professionals to deliver a psychologically-based intervention for people with COPD: results from the TANDEM study. NPJ Primary Care Respiratory Medicine 35, 11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41533-025-00416-y
title: Cognitive First Aid Rating Scale (CFARs) for therapeutic competence of newly trained CBT-naive professionals
description: The CFARs is a validated 10-item scale (Cronbach's Alpha 0.93), adapted from Blackburn's revised Cognitive Rating Scale, for rating the skills of newly trained "CBT-naïve" healthcare professionals delivering psychological support. Each item is scored zero (poor skills) to six (high skill); "A total score of >30 and three or above on any item is considered to reflect therapeutic competence." Items cover focus/structure, pacing, chunking/feedback, integration of CBT into the professional model, collaborative relationship, guided discovery, interpersonal effectiveness, eliciting model components, change techniques and closure.
requirements: Rating by an assessor trained in psychological interventions, ideally blind to facilitator identity and outcomes
Completion for each session within a therapy series so case-level averages can be calculated
target_learners: Healthcare professionals newly trained in cognitive behavioural approaches
target_learning_goals: Assessing and developing therapeutic delivery competence
examples: Used in TANDEM to rate 180 audio-recorded sessions, yielding a mean total of 35.5 (SD 7.0)
key_sources: Wileman V., Steed L., Pinnock H., Kelly M., Sohanpal R., Heslop-Marshall K., Taylor SJC. (2025). Assessing competence of primary care respiratory healthcare professionals to deliver a psychologically-based intervention for people with COPD: results from the TANDEM study. NPJ Primary Care Respiratory Medicine 35, 11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41533-025-00416-y

article_title: Barriers and facilitators to interprofessional simulation-based learning in a Ugandan medical school: a qualitative study.
citation: Najjuma Josephine N., Muhumuza Albert, Santorino Data, Sekyere Samuel Owusu, Ocheke Amaka N., Yiltok Simon J., Bajunirwe Francis. (2024). Barriers and facilitators to interprofessional simulation-based learning in a Ugandan medical school: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06521-9
title: Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) as the organizing framework for identifying Sim-IPE barriers and facilitators
description: The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is an implementation-research framework the authors used to structure data collection and deductive coding of barriers and facilitators to simulation-enhanced interprofessional education. The study states it was "Guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR)", and results mapped onto "the six CFIR domains namely, the intervention characteristics, inner setting, outer setting, individual characteristics and the process." A semi-structured tool was designed using CFIR constructs, and a priori themes were generated from CFIR-based research questions alongside emerging themes.
requirements: Data collection tools and codes structured around CFIR constructs, as the study's semi-structured tool was designed using the constructs of the CFIR tool
constraints: The article reports barriers and facilitators arising from five named CFIR domains for one Ugandan medical school context; findings are offered as a benchmark for other low- and middle-income countries rather than a generalizable result
target_learners: Undergraduate medical and nursing students in their clinical years
examples: Nine key informant interviews and three uniprofessional focus group discussions were coded deductively using CFIR-driven codes, with themes summarized in the article's Table 2
key_sources: Najjuma Josephine N., Muhumuza Albert, Santorino Data, Sekyere Samuel Owusu, Ocheke Amaka N., Yiltok Simon J., Bajunirwe Francis. (2024). Barriers and facilitators to interprofessional simulation-based learning in a Ugandan medical school: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06521-9
